--- title: "Methods for Generating Random Variables 🎲" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # Methods for Generating Random Variables

Lecture A: pseudo-random numbers, sampling, inverse transform, acceptance-rejection

Lecture B: transformations, sums and mixtures, multivariate normal, the sphere

::: notes - Rizzo Chapter 3. Two 75-minute lectures. Part A ends after acceptance-rejection (Example 3.8 can be started if time permits). - Every generator we write is validated: compare to the theoretical density/pmf, QQ-plots, and moments. ::: # Lecture A: Inverse Transform and Acceptance-Rejection {#part-a} ## Why Generate Random Variables? - Every simulation in this course (Monte Carlo integration, power studies, bootstrap, MCMC) needs random variates from a specified distribution. - R already has `rnorm`, `rgamma`, `rbeta`, ... **but** + many distributions of interest have no built-in generator (mixtures, truncated, multivariate, user-defined), + knowing *how* generators work tells you when they are efficient and when they fail. - Everything starts from **Uniform(0,1)** pseudo-random numbers. ## Pseudo-Random Numbers - Computers produce deterministic sequences that *look* iid Uniform(0,1). - R's default is the Mersenne-Twister (period $2^{19937}-1$); see `?RNGkind`. - `set.seed()` makes a simulation reproducible. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} RNGkind() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Mersenne-Twister" "Inversion" "Rejection" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); u1 <- runif(3) set.seed(4750); u2 <- runif(3) identical(u1, u2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: A toy **linear congruential generator** $x_{k+1} = (a x_k + c) \bmod m$, $u_k = x_k/m$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lcg <- function(n, seed = 1, a = 16807, c = 0, m = 2^31 - 1) { x <- numeric(n); x[1] <- seed for (k in 2:n) x[k] <- (a * x[k - 1] + c) %% m x / m } round(lcg(6, seed = 4750), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.0000 0.0372 0.8045 0.1253 0.5881 0.6444 ``` ::: ::: ## Sampling from a Finite Population (Example 3.1) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) sample(0:1, size = 10, replace = TRUE) # toss some coins ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 0 0 0 1 1 0 0 0 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sample(1:100, size = 6, replace = FALSE) # lottery numbers ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 30 45 38 51 40 35 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sample(toupper(letters)) # a random permutation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "H" "X" "D" "R" "K" "V" "Q" "A" "S" "L" "Y" "T" "I" "C" "B" "J" "Z" "F" "W" [20] "G" "P" "E" "O" "N" "M" "U" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <- sample(1:3, size = 100, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.2, .3, .5)) table(x) # multinomial sampling ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x 1 2 3 26 18 56 ``` ::: ::: ## The Inverse Transform Method ::: fact **Probability integral transformation.** If $X$ is continuous with cdf $F_X$, then $U = F_X(X)\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)$. ::: Define $F_X^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x: F_X(x) = u\}$, $0(u) | |:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------| |Exponential() |1 - exp(-x) |-log(1-u)/ | |Pareto(a, b) |1 - (b/x)^a, x b |b (1-u)^(-1/a) | |Cauchy(, ) |1/2 + arctan((x-)/)/ | + tan((u - 1/2)) | |Logistic |1/(1 + exp(-x)) |log(u/(1-u)) | |Weibull(k, ) |1 - exp(-(x/)^k) |(-log(1-u))^(1/k) | |Rayleigh() |1 - exp(-x/(2)) | sqrt(-2 log(1-u)) | ::: ::: ::: question Which common continuous distributions do **not** have a closed-form $F^{-1}$? (Normal, gamma, beta, ...) We need other methods for these. ::: ## Inverse Transform: Discrete Case If $\cdots < x_{i-1} < x_i < \cdots$ are the points of discontinuity of $F_X$, then $F_X^{-1}(u) = x_i$ where $F_X(x_{i-1}) < u \le F_X(x_i)$. ::: algo For each random variate: generate $u\sim$ Uniform(0,1) and deliver $x_i$ such that $F(x_{i-1}) < u \le F(x_i)$. ::: **Example 3.4 (two-point distribution).** $P(X=1) = p = 0.4$, $P(X=0) = 0.6$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1000; p <- 0.4 u <- runif(n) x <- as.integer(u > 0.6) # (u > 0.6) is a logical vector c(mean = mean(x), var = var(x), theory_var = p * (1 - p)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean var theory_var 0.4020 0.2406 0.2400 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 3.5: Geometric Distribution $f(x) = pq^x$, $x = 0,1,2,\dots$ and $F(x) = 1-q^{x+1}$. Solve $1 - q^x < u \le 1 - q^{x+1}$: $$ x = \lceil \log(1-u)/\log(q)\rceil - 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \lfloor \log(u)/\log(q)\rfloor\ \ (\text{since } 1-U\sim U) $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1e4; p <- 0.25 x <- floor(log(runif(n)) / log(1 - p)) k <- 0:15 barplot(rbind(table(factor(x, levels = k)) / n, dgeom(k, p)), beside = TRUE, names.arg = k, col = c("#FFCC00", "#003366"), legend.text = c("generated", "dgeom"), main = "Geometric(0.25)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 3.6: Logarithmic Distribution $$ f(x) = \frac{a\,\theta^x}{x},\quad x = 1,2,\dots,\quad a = \big(-\log(1-\theta)\big)^{-1} $$ - No closed-form inverse. Store the cdf on a grid; `sum(u > F) + 1` counts how many $F(x) < u$. - Compute $f(x)$ as `exp(log(a) + x*log(theta) - log(x))` for numerical accuracy. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rlogarithmic <- function(n, theta) { u <- runif(n) N <- ceiling(-16 / log10(theta)) # initial length of cdf vector k <- 1:N a <- -1 / log(1 - theta) fk <- exp(log(a) + k * log(theta) - log(k)) Fk <- cumsum(fk) x <- integer(n) for (i in 1:n) { x[i] <- as.integer(sum(u[i] > Fk)) # F^{-1}(u) - 1 while (x[i] == N) { # extend the cdf if needed logf <- log(a) + (N + 1) * log(theta) - log(N + 1) fk <- c(fk, exp(logf)); Fk <- c(Fk, Fk[N] + fk[N + 1]); N <- N + 1 x[i] <- as.integer(sum(u[i] > Fk)) } } x + 1 } ``` ::: ## Checking the Logarithmic Generator ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1000; theta <- 0.5 x <- rlogarithmic(n, theta) k <- sort(unique(x)) p <- -1 / log(1 - theta) * theta^k / k se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n) round(rbind(observed = table(x) / n, p = p, se = se), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 observed 0.720 0.173 0.057 0.028 0.010 0.007 0.004 0.001 p 0.721 0.180 0.060 0.023 0.009 0.004 0.002 0.001 se 0.014 0.012 0.008 0.005 0.003 0.002 0.001 0.001 ``` ::: ::: The observed relative frequencies are within about two standard errors of the theoretical probabilities. # The Acceptance-Rejection Method ## The Acceptance-Rejection Method Suppose $X$ has density (pmf) $f$, $Y$ has density $g$, and there is a constant $c$ with $$ \frac{f(t)}{g(t)} \le c\quad\text{for all } t \text{ with } f(t) > 0. $$ ::: algo 1. Find $Y\sim g$ (easy to generate) with $f(t)/g(t)\le c$. 2. For each variate required: a. Generate $y$ from $g$. b. Generate $u$ from Uniform(0,1). c. If $u < f(y)/(c\,g(y))$, accept $y$ and deliver $x = y$; otherwise reject $y$ and repeat from 2a. ::: ## Why It Works, and How Efficient It Is - $P(\text{accept}\mid Y) = P\big(U < \tfrac{f(Y)}{cg(Y)}\mid Y\big) = \dfrac{f(Y)}{cg(Y)}$ - Overall acceptance probability: $\displaystyle\sum_y \frac{f(y)}{cg(y)}g(y) = \frac1c$ - Number of iterations until acceptance $\sim$ Geometric with mean $c$ $\Rightarrow$ want $c$ **small**. - **Bayes:** $P(k\mid\text{accepted}) = \dfrac{P(\text{accepted}\mid k)g(k)}{P(\text{accepted})} = \dfrac{[f(k)/(cg(k))]g(k)}{1/c} = f(k)$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 3.7: Beta(2, 2) by Acceptance-Rejection $f(x) = 6x(1-x)$, $0 u. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) n <- 1000; k <- 0; j <- 0; y <- numeric(n) while (k < n) { u <- runif(1) j <- j + 1 x <- runif(1) # random variate from g if (x * (1 - x) > u) { # we accept x k <- k + 1 y[k] <- x } } j # iterations: expect about c * n = 6000 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5880 ``` ::: ::: ## Checking the Sample ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- seq(.1, .9, .1) Qhat <- quantile(y, p) # quantiles of the sample Q <- qbeta(p, 2, 2) # theoretical quantiles se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / (n * dbeta(Q, 2, 2)^2)) round(rbind(Qhat, Q, se), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 10% 20% 30% 40% 50% 60% 70% 80% 90% Qhat 0.180 0.274 0.351 0.424 0.493 0.564 0.641 0.723 0.820 Q 0.196 0.287 0.363 0.433 0.500 0.567 0.637 0.713 0.804 se 0.010 0.010 0.010 0.011 0.011 0.011 0.010 0.010 0.010 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hist(y, prob = TRUE, breaks = 30, col = "#FFCC00", main = "Beta(2,2) by acceptance-rejection") curve(dbeta(x, 2, 2), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "#003366") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## A Vectorized Acceptance-Rejection ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rAR <- function(n, f, rg, dg, c) { out <- numeric(0); tries <- 0 while (length(out) < n) { m <- ceiling(1.2 * c * (n - length(out))) # propose in batches y <- rg(m); u <- runif(m); tries <- tries + m out <- c(out, y[u < f(y) / (c * dg(y))]) } structure(out[1:n], acceptance = n / tries) } set.seed(4750) z <- rAR(1e4, f = function(x) 6 * x * (1 - x), rg = runif, dg = dunif, c = 1.5) attr(z, "acceptance") # close to 1/c = 0.667 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5556 ``` ::: ::: ::: your-turn Use acceptance-rejection with a **Cauchy** proposal to generate standard normal variates. What is the smallest valid $c$? ::: # Lecture B: Transformations, Mixtures, Multivariate {#part-b} ## Transformation Methods Many distributions are related by transformations: 1. $Z\sim N(0,1)\Rightarrow V = Z^2\sim\chi^2(1)$. 2. $U\sim\chi^2(m)$, $V\sim\chi^2(n)$ independent $\Rightarrow F = \dfrac{U/m}{V/n}\sim F(m,n)$. 3. $Z\sim N(0,1)$, $V\sim\chi^2(n)$ independent $\Rightarrow T = \dfrac{Z}{\sqrt{V/n}}\sim t(n)$. 4. $U, V\iid$ Uniform(0,1) $\Rightarrow$ (**Box-Muller**) $$ Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\log U}\cos(2\pi V),\quad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\log U}\sin(2\pi V)\ \ \iid N(0,1). $$ 5. $U\sim\text{Gamma}(r,\lambda)$, $V\sim\text{Gamma}(s,\lambda)$ independent $\Rightarrow X = \dfrac{U}{U+V}\sim\text{Beta}(r,s)$. ## Box-Muller ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 5000 u <- runif(n); v <- runif(n) z1 <- sqrt(-2 * log(u)) * cos(2 * pi * v) z2 <- sqrt(-2 * log(u)) * sin(2 * pi * v) c(mean(z1), sd(z1), cor(z1, z2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.003788 0.996780 0.013924 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) qqnorm(z1, pch = "."); qqline(z1, col = 2, lwd = 2) plot(z1, z2, pch = 20, col = "#00336640", asp = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 3.8: Beta from Gammas ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1000; a <- 3; b <- 2 u <- rgamma(n, shape = a, rate = 1) v <- rgamma(n, shape = b, rate = 1) x <- u / (u + v) q <- qbeta(ppoints(n), a, b) qqplot(q, x, cex = 0.5, xlab = "Beta(3, 2)", ylab = "Sample", main = "QQ plot: U/(U+V)") abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 3.9: Logarithmic Distribution, Version 2 If $U, V\iid$ Uniform(0,1), then $X = \left\lfloor 1 + \dfrac{\log V}{\log\big(1-(1-\theta)^U\big)}\right\rfloor\sim$ Logarithmic($\theta$). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1000; theta <- 0.5 u <- runif(n); v <- runif(n) x <- floor(1 + log(v) / log(1 - (1 - theta)^u)) k <- 1:max(x) p <- -1 / log(1 - theta) * theta^k / k round(rbind(observed = table(factor(x, levels = k)) / n, theory = p), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 observed 0.716 0.185 0.065 0.020 0.008 0.004 0.000 0.002 theory 0.721 0.180 0.060 0.023 0.009 0.004 0.002 0.001 ``` ::: ::: - Fully vectorized: no loops, no stored cdf. Much faster than Example 3.6. ## Example 3.10: Chi-square as a Sum of Squares $\chi^2(\nu)$ = sum of $\nu$ squared iid $N(0,1)$. Fill an $n\times\nu$ matrix with $n\nu$ normals and take row sums of squares. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1000; nu <- 2 X <- matrix(rnorm(n * nu), n, nu)^2 # matrix of squared normals y <- rowSums(X) # sum the squared normals across each row c(mean = mean(y), mean_theory = nu, E_y2 = mean(y^2), E_y2_theory = 2 * nu + nu^2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean mean_theory E_y2 E_y2_theory 1.936 2.000 7.488 8.000 ``` ::: ::: ::: tip `rowSums()` and `colSums()` are much faster than `apply(X, 1, sum)` (we benchmark this in Ch 15). ::: ## Sums (Convolutions) and Mixtures - **Convolution:** $S = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ for independent $X_j$; e.g. $\chi^2(\nu)$, Gamma$(n,\lambda)$ = sum of exponentials, NegBin$(r,p)$ = sum of geometrics. - **Mixture:** $F_X(x) = \sum_i \theta_i F_{X_i}(x)$ with $\theta_i > 0$, $\sum\theta_i = 1$ (discrete mixture), or $F_X(x) = \int F_{X\mid Y=y}(x) f_Y(y)\,dy$ (continuous mixture). ::: alert A convolution adds the **random variables**; a mixture averages the **distributions**. To generate a mixture: first draw the component label, then draw from that component. ::: ## Example 3.11: Convolution vs. Mixture $X_1\sim\text{Gamma}(2,2)$, $X_2\sim\text{Gamma}(2,4)$; compare $S = X_1 + X_2$ with $F_X = 0.5F_{X_1} + 0.5F_{X_2}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1000 x1 <- rgamma(n, 2, 2); x2 <- rgamma(n, 2, 4) s <- x1 + x2 # the convolution u <- runif(n); k <- as.integer(u > 0.5) # vector of 0's and 1's x <- k * x1 + (1 - k) * x2 # the mixture par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) hist(s, prob = TRUE, breaks = 30, col = "#88A0C8", main = "Convolution") hist(x, prob = TRUE, breaks = 30, col = "#FFCC00", main = "Mixture") curve(0.5 * dgamma(x, 2, 2) + 0.5 * dgamma(x, 2, 4), add = TRUE, lwd = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Examples 3.12 - 3.14: Mixture of Several Gammas $F_X = \sum_{j=1}^5\theta_jF_{X_j}$, $X_j\sim\text{Gamma}(r = 3, \lambda_j = 1/j)$, $\theta_j = j/15$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 5000 k <- sample(1:5, size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = (1:5) / 15) # component labels rate <- 1 / k x <- rgamma(n, shape = 3, rate = rate) f <- function(x) sapply(x, function(xi) sum((1:5) / 15 * dgamma(xi, 3, 1 / (1:5)))) hist(x, prob = TRUE, breaks = 60, col = "#FFCC00", main = "Mixture of 5 gammas", xlim = c(0, 40)) for (j in 1:5) curve(dgamma(x, 3, 1 / j), add = TRUE, col = "gray50", lty = 2) curve(f(x), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "#003366") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 3.15: Poisson-Gamma Mixture If $X\mid\Lambda = \lambda\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ and $\Lambda\sim\text{Gamma}(r,\beta)$, then $X\sim\text{NegBin}(r, p = \beta/(1+\beta))$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 1000; r <- 4; beta <- 3 lambda <- rgamma(n, r, beta) # lambda is random x <- rpois(n, lambda) # the mixture mix <- tabulate(x + 1) / n negbin <- round(dnbinom(0:max(x), r, beta / (1 + beta)), 3) se <- sqrt(negbin * (1 - negbin) / n) round(rbind(mix, negbin, se), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] [,8] mix 0.311 0.331 0.203 0.091 0.039 0.019 0.004 0.002 negbin 0.316 0.316 0.198 0.099 0.043 0.017 0.006 0.002 se 0.015 0.015 0.013 0.009 0.006 0.004 0.002 0.001 ``` ::: ::: # Multivariate Distributions ## Generating Multivariate Normal Vectors If $\bZ\sim N_d(\mathbf 0,\bI_d)$ and $\bSigma = \mathbf C\mathbf C^\T$, then $\bX = \mathbf C\bZ + \bmu\sim N_d(\bmu,\bSigma)$. For a matrix of $n$ rows: $$ \bX = \bZ\,\mathbf Q + \mathbf J\bmu^\T,\qquad \mathbf Q^\T\mathbf Q = \bSigma. $$ Three factorizations of $\bSigma$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Method |Factorization |R | |:------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------| |Spectral (Ex 3.16) | = P P, Q = P ^ P |`eigen()` | |SVD (Ex 3.17) | = U D V, Q = U D^ V |`svd()` | |Choleski (Ex 3.18) | = Q Q, Q upper triangular |`chol()` | ::: ::: ## Examples 3.16 - 3.18: Three Generators ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rmvn.eigen <- function(n, mu, Sigma) { d <- length(mu); ev <- eigen(Sigma, symmetric = TRUE) Q <- ev$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(ev$values)) %*% t(ev$vectors) Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * d), nrow = n, ncol = d) Z %*% Q + matrix(mu, n, d, byrow = TRUE) } rmvn.svd <- function(n, mu, Sigma) { d <- length(mu); S <- svd(Sigma) Q <- S$u %*% diag(sqrt(S$d)) %*% t(S$v) Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * d), nrow = n, ncol = d) Z %*% Q + matrix(mu, n, d, byrow = TRUE) } rmvn.Choleski <- function(n, mu, Sigma) { d <- length(mu); Q <- chol(Sigma) # Choleski factorization of Sigma Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * d), nrow = n, ncol = d) Z %*% Q + matrix(mu, n, d, byrow = TRUE) } mu <- c(0, 1, 2); Sigma <- matrix(c(1, -.5, .5, -.5, 1, -.5, .5, -.5, 1), 3) set.seed(4750); X <- rmvn.Choleski(5000, mu, Sigma) round(colMeans(X), 2); round(cor(X), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.02 1.01 2.00 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1.00 -0.50 0.49 [2,] -0.50 1.00 -0.49 [3,] 0.49 -0.49 1.00 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 3.19: Comparing Performance ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(100); n <- 100; d <- 30; N <- 2000 mu <- numeric(d); Sigma <- cov(matrix(rnorm(n * d), n, d)) # a 30 x 30 covariance timing <- rbind( eigen = system.time(for (i in 1:N) rmvn.eigen(n, mu, Sigma))[1:3], svd = system.time(for (i in 1:N) rmvn.svd(n, mu, Sigma))[1:3], Choleski = system.time(for (i in 1:N) rmvn.Choleski(n, mu, Sigma))[1:3], MASS = system.time(for (i in 1:N) MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu, Sigma))[1:3]) timing ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` user.self sys.self elapsed eigen 0.716 0.01 0.856 svd 0.837 0.00 0.859 Choleski 0.374 0.00 0.377 MASS 0.702 0.00 0.712 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - Choleski is usually fastest. MASS::mvrnorm uses the eigen decomposition (and handles positive semi-definite Sigma). mvtnorm::rmvnorm offers all three. ::: ## Example 3.20: Multivariate Normal Location Mixture $p N_d(\bmu_1,\bSigma) + (1-p)N_d(\bmu_2,\bSigma)$ with $\bmu_1 = \mathbf 0$, $\bmu_2 = (2,\dots,2)$, $\bSigma = \bI$, $p = 0.5$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} loc.mix <- function(n, p, mu1, mu2, Sigma) { n1 <- rbinom(1, size = n, prob = p); n2 <- n - n1 x <- rbind(MASS::mvrnorm(n1, mu1, Sigma), MASS::mvrnorm(n2, mu2, Sigma)) x[sample(1:n), ] # mix them } set.seed(4750) x <- loc.mix(1000, .5, rep(0, 4), rep(2, 4), diag(4)) par(mfrow = c(1, 4)) for (i in 1:4) hist(x[, i], prob = TRUE, breaks = 30, main = paste0("X", i), col = "#FFCC00", xlab = "") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Example 3.21: Uniform on the Sphere If $\bZ\sim N_d(\mathbf 0,\bI_d)$, then $\bZ/\|\bZ\|$ is uniformly distributed on the unit sphere $S^{d-1}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} runif.sphere <- function(n, d) { M <- matrix(rnorm(n * d), nrow = n, ncol = d) L <- function(x) sqrt(sum(x * x)) # length of a vector M / apply(M, 1, L) } set.seed(4750) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) X <- runif.sphere(200, 2); plot(X, asp = 1, pch = 19, cex = .6, col = "#003366", main = "d = 2") X <- runif.sphere(2000, 3) scatterplot <- function(X) { # a rotated 2-d view of the 3-d points R <- qr.Q(qr(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 0, 1, -1, 1, 0, 0), 3))) P <- X %*% R; plot(P[, 1:2], asp = 1, pch = 20, cex = .5, col = ifelse(P[, 3] > 0, "#C2185B", "gray70"), main = "d = 3 (front hemisphere in pink)") } scatterplot(X) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/06-rv-gen/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python Supplement: Generators in `numpy` ```{.python} import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(4750) u = rng.uniform(size=5000) x = -np.log(u) / 2 # inverse transform: Exp(rate = 2) Sigma = np.array([[1, .8], [.8, 1]]) Z = rng.standard_normal((5000, 2)) X = Z @ np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma).T # Choleski: rows ~ N(0, Sigma) print(x.mean(), np.cov(X, rowvar=False)) ``` ## Summary ::: instructions - **Inverse transform:** $X = F^{-1}(U)$; discrete: $x_i$ with $F(x_{i-1}) < u\le F(x_i)$. - **Acceptance-rejection:** propose from $g$, accept with probability $f/(cg)$; expected $c$ proposals per variate. - **Transformations:** Box-Muller, $\chi^2$, $t$, $F$, beta from gammas. - **Sums vs. mixtures:** add random variables vs. average distributions. - **Multivariate normal:** $\bZ\mathbf Q + \bmu$ with spectral, SVD, or Choleski factor; normalize normals for the sphere. - Always **validate** a generator: histogram + density, QQ-plot, moments, frequency tables with SEs. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
